Norway, Sweden and Finland share long borders and similar geography, including vast rural areas with limited health care resources. Finland operates a centralized blood service, whereas Norway and Sweden maintain decentralized systems, with regional authorities responsible for their own blood supply. All three countries adhere to a total defence concept, wherein military forces depend on civilian transfusion services. In mass casualty events, the demand for transfusion services to provide urgent blood and blood components is expected to be high. Haemorrhage remains the leading cause of preventable prehospital death in trauma cases, and the availability of blood products in prehospital settings is critical in both civilian and military environments. Key priorities identified include: establishing stockpiles of shelf-stable blood products, developing surge capacity plans for rapid upscaling of blood collection and whole blood and component production, conducting joint training and exercises involving blood establishments, transfusion services, hospitals and military units, and collaboration in a pilot cross-border initiative-the Nordic Blood Preparedness Project-in northern Norway, Sweden and Finland, aimed at harmonizing regulations and procedures during emergencies. To effectively save lives during disasters and armed conflicts, it is essential to have well-documented and operational blood preparedness plans in place.

Challenging the Nordic model? The cultural policies of populist parties in Finland and Sweden
Olli Jakonen, Vappu Renko & Tobias Harding
Abstract
Cultural policy is increasingly re-politicised by populism amid shifting political discourse in Europe
and beyond. This article investigates the re-politicisation of cultural policy in Sweden and Finland,
set against the backdrop of rising populism, which is potentially reshaping the traditionally stable
Nordic cultural policy landscape. It focuses on the cultural policies of two populist parties: the
Finns Party in Finland and the Sweden Democrats in Sweden. Employing qualitative analysis of
party programs, this study reveals both parties’ opposition to several aspects of the Nordic cultural
policy model. The parties advocate for ‘regular people’ as opposed to the ‘elite’ and emphasise
national identity over economy-driven policies, marking a shift from the neoliberal tendencies of
the past decades. Our analysis highlights the role of these parties in politicising culture and
challenging the long-standing consensus in Nordic cultural policies. These findings shed light on
the evolving dynamics of Nordic cultural policy under growing populist influence.
Keywords
Populism, Cultural Politics, Sweden Democrats, Finns Party, Nordic Model

Introduction
In many Western societies, cultural policy has become increasingly politicised, as the cultural
aspects of politics have become increasingly pronounced (e.g. Harding 2022; Rius-Ulldemolins and
Rubio-Arostegui 2022; Sivonen and Purhonen 2021). This politicisation appears to reflect a broader
shift in political discourse which has been identified in recent research on populism’s impact on
various dimensions of polity, policies and politics (Caiani and Graziano 2022). The
(re)politicisation of cultural policy has been fuelled by the rise of populism, which is increasingly
seen as a significant challenge to established democratic politics (Caramani 2017; Mudde 2019;
Mudde and Kaltwasser 2017; Norris and Inglehart 2019). Nationalist populism, in particular, has
placed strong emphasis on cultural values and identities as the basis for cultural policies (Moran and
Littler 2020).
Populist tendencies have also become visible in the Nordic countries, where cultural policy
structures were broadly established during the emergence of the welfare state after WWII (Mangset
et al. 2008; Sokka et al. 2022). Despite the different historical backgrounds and institutional
contexts of the Nordic countries, they share many similar features that have been categorised as a
distinct ‘Nordic cultural policy model’. This model includes established national and local
administration for cultural services, powerful interest organisations, the application of the arm’s
length principle, and, in some cases, strong legislative frameworks (Kangas and Vestheim 2010;
Mangset 2015; Saukkonen 2021). Consensus-orientation is also a distinct feature: coalition

Abstract
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine profoundly disrupted Arctic governance, challenging the
long-standing notion of Arctic exceptionalism and creating enduring turbulence. While
scholarly debate has largely focused on geopolitical and institutional consequences, the local-
level impacts remain underexamined. This study investigates adaptive governance (AG)
responses to the war’s effects in Norway’s northernmost counties, Troms and Finnmark, which
share a direct border with Russia. The analysis draws on the concepts of crisis, turbulence, and
AG, situating them within broader scholarship on how decision-making сenters respond to
crises and turbulence and political adaptation. It examines stakeholder responses across four
key domains: civilian preparedness, international cooperation, infrastructure development, and
the economic repercussions of sanctions. Based on 19 semi-structured interviews, policy
documents, and media analysis, the study reveals both adaptation and persistent challenges
shaped by pre-existing governance structures, demographic and economic conditions, and past
cooperation with Russia. The study contributes to AG literature by unpacking the interplay
between strategies, highlighting structural constraints, and demonstrating how geopolitical
disruptions shape local governance in strategically significant environments.

Perspectives on Arctic Security: An Analysis of
Strategies, Presence, and Capabilities from Ten Arctic
and Non-arctic Countries
Abstract
The accelerating impacts of climate change and intensifying geopolitical interests have posi-
tioned the Arctic as a critical arena for strategic competition, resource extraction, and envi-
ronmental governance. In response, countries with Arctic interests have increasingly adopted
national strategies that articulate security priorities across geopolitical, economic, and environ-
mental dimensions, among others. Yet, despite the growing salience of Arctic security, exist-
ing scholarship remains fragmented and predominantly qualitative, offering limited systematic,
data-driven cross-national comparisons of Arctic strategies. This study addresses these gaps by
examining the Arctic policy documents of the eight Arctic states – Canada, Denmark, Finland,
Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, and the United States – alongside observer states China and
India. Using 107 Arctic policy documents from ten countries and a human-led, AI-assisted
text-mining workflow, we quantify and compare national security priorities across countries.
The analysis reveals broad consensus on climate and environmental concerns, but sharp diver-
gences in territorial and resource-related strategies: for example, the United States and Russia
emphasize sovereignty, whereas Finland advocates demilitarization. Moreover, larger states
such as Canada, Russia, and the United States feature prominently in other countries’ pol-
icy documents, while smaller Arctic states attract comparatively limited attention. Through a
novel, data-driven comparison of Arctic security strategies, this study advances understanding
of Arctic security governance and offers insights for policy development.
Keywords: Arctic security, security strategy, defense, artificial intelligence, Arctic policy

TITLE:
Nordic Defense Architecture Convergence and NATO Alignment: The Norway-Finland Strategic Recalibration

---

THROUGH LINE:
Finland and Norway have structurally converged within NATO to counter shared Russian threats, but institutional path dependencies and hybrid vulnerability exposure will fracture coordination before 2030 unless governance friction is resolved.

---

VERDICT:
Finland and Norway have recently adapted their defense and security architectures in response to shared geopolitical threats, moving toward closer alignment with NATO and deeper regional coordination. This is not a marginal adjustment — it is a structural transformation. Finland's accession to NATO in 2023 [SRC-20] ended a non-alignment tradition that had defined Finnish security policy for decades, a shift forced by Russia's demonstrated willingness to violate sovereignty since 2008 and its full-scale invasion of Ukraine [SRC-15]. Norway, already a NATO member, has accelerated its defense spending trajectory toward 3.5% of GDP by 2035, with 1.62 trillion NOK allocated over 2025-2036 [SRC-31], and signed the Norwegian-French 'Narvik' defense agreement in 2026, introducing French nuclear deterrence posture into Arctic security architecture [SRC-31]. Total defence has reemerged as the central organizing principle across Finland, Norway, and Sweden [SRC-20], with the three countries moving toward closer alignment, deeper interoperability, and increasingly transnational coordination [SRC-20]. The Støre-Stubb conversation at the Council on Foreign Relations [SRC-2] signals elite consensus on these priorities, though elite discourse reveals intentions and framing, not policy outcomes — a distinction that domain experts flagged as a category error common in policy analysis [SRC-2]. The central finding is that this convergence is real but structurally incomplete: persistent institutional path dependencies produce divergent national total defence architectures despite convergent threat perceptions [SRC-22]. Finland retains a strongly centralized system, Norway emphasizes subsidiarity and layered coordination, and Sweden combines a decentralized administrative tradition with renewed recentralization [SRC-20]. These divergent architectures create coordination friction under shared NATO command that will intensify as integration deepens. Simultaneously, the security gains from NATO accession are asymmetric: conventional deterrence improves while exposure to hybrid provocations operating below the Article 5 threshold increases [SRC-5][SRC-15]. Russia's military deployments in the North have decreased from February 2022 to end of 2024 [SRC-19], but this restraint is contingent on Ukraine resource constraints, not strategic acquiescence. You are the editorial arbiter at NomosX — the institute's final decision voice. Voice: Harvard Kennedy School Policy Memo + notes of McKinsey Global Institute.

THE NOMOSX EDITORIAL DNA — read this before writing anything.

You are not writing a report. You are performing an act of ordering.
"From Chaos to Nomos" is not a tagline — it is the movement your text must embody.

THE MANIFESTO:
The world doesn't suffer from a lack of information. It suffers from a lack of structure.
Knowledge without order creates noise. Order without verification creates opinion.
Verification without scenarios creates hindsight. We bind all three.
That is NomosX.

OUR DNA IS PROSPECTIVE.
NomosX is not an analytical think tank that happens to do foresight.
NomosX is a FORESIGHT INSTITUTE that grounds its foresight in rigorous analysis.
The prospective dimension — scenarios, base rates, signals, cross-impact, sensitivity —
is not an appendix to our reports. It is the heart of what we do.
Every report must answer not just "what is happening?" but "what could happen,
with what probability, and what should we do about it NOW?"
Our foresight is PhD-level: Delphi expert calibration, Monte Carlo simulation,
Fermi decomposition, base rates from historical analogues, cross-impact balance,
extremizing functions, Platt scaling, bootstrap confidence intervals.
But we present this rigor as NARRATIVE, not as a dashboard.
The numbers support the story. The story makes the numbers intelligible.

THE SIX PILLARS (every position must reflect these):
1. TRANSFORM CHAOS INTO ORDER — Structure the noise into a causal chain anyone can follow.
2. MEANING BEFORE ANSWERS — Define the question before you answer it. A precise question poorly answered beats a vague one answered confidently.
3. MAP KNOWLEDGE, DON'T ACCUMULATE IT — Show where evidence is dense, absent, or contradictory. The map is the product.
4. CONNECT IDEAS ACROSS DOMAINS — The most consequential insights live at the intersection. Force the collision.
5. SCENARIOS, NOT SINGLE FORECASTS — Multiple futures, each with a probability, each as a narrative. The world doesn't move in straight lines. This is our DNA.
6. COMBAT NOVLANGUE, GUARD THE TRUTH — Plain words. No buzzwords. No corporate-speak. No academic hedging. Say what you mean.

THE VOICE:
- POSITIONS, NOT OPINIONS. We commit to a view. We state what we believe and why. We do not hide behind "it could be argued that" or "some analysts suggest." We say: "We believe X. Here is why. Here is what would change our mind."
- CONFIDENT BUT NOT DOGMATIC. "We believe X, with confidence Y" — not "X is true." Acknowledge uncertainty without hiding behind it. Provisional but committed.
- HIGH-LEVEL BUT ACCESSIBLE. We write for decision-makers who think at the frontier. Intellectual ambition without academic jargon. Conceptual depth without abstraction. We are the institute that makes complex foresight intelligible to people who sign decisions.
- LITERARY BUT NOT DECORATIVE. Every sentence does double duty: advances the argument AND pleases the ear. Vary sentence rhythm — short punchy sentences mixed with longer subordinate clauses. Never write two consecutive sentences of the same length.
- PLAIN WORDS, DEEP THOUGHTS. Prefer everyday speech over jargon. Short words over long. Active over passive. But embrace complexity of thought, not simplification. (Orwell: "Never use a long word where a short one will do.")
- ANTI-NOVLANGUE. Ban: "leverage" (as verb), "synergy", "paradigm shift", "game-changer", "value proposition", "deep dive", "double down", "move the needle", "at the end of the day", "stakeholder engagement", "capacity building", "robust framework", "holistic approach". If you catch yourself writing one of these, stop and say what you actually mean.
- SKIN IN THE GAME. Take intellectual risk. The document is a conversation, not a pronouncement. The reader can push back, probe the logic, find the assumptions, stress-test the conclusion.

THE NOMOS ARC (the structure of every position):
Every NomosX report moves through four phases — the same four phases as our method: Map · Confront · Quantify · Decide.
- ACT I — THE QUESTION (Map): Define the question precisely. Show the chaos. What is known, what is disputed, what is absent?
- ACT II — THE EVIDENCE (Confront): State our position. Show why we believe it. Force the strongest counter-argument. The friction is the point.
- ACT III — THE FUTURES (Quantify): THIS IS OUR DNA. A dedicated prospective space with:
  (a) The Foresight Framework — horizon, base rate context, Fermi decomposition, key uncertainties, cross-impact, snow leopards (underappreciated phenomena that could have outsized impact), methodology note.
  (b) The Scenarios — each as a NARRATIVE set in the future tense ("By 2030, the alliance has settled into..."), not bullet points. With: probability, 90% CI, base rate, calibrated probability, sensitivity, key drivers, blockers, uncertainty drivers, tipping point, cross-impact, signals.
  (c) The Trajectory — where things are heading, the path dependency.
  (d) What We Ruled Out — rejected alternatives with reasoning and residual risk.
  (e) Signals to Watch — early warning indicators that would shift probability.
- ACT IV — THE DECISION (Decide): A clear position, with confidence. Sources visible. Doubts logged. What would change our mind. The strongest objection, answered.

THE PROSPECTIVE MUST BE PhD-LEVEL:
- Base rates: "Historically, regime transitions in petrostates occur within 18 months of a succession crisis in 67% of cases [SRC-N]. Our base rate is 0.67."
- Fermi decomposition: "The question decomposes into three sub-questions: (1) Will the succession occur? (2) Will it be contested? (3) Will the contestation trigger a transition? Each estimated independently."
- Expert calibration: "Five Delphi experts, weighted by inverse distance from median, converged on 0.42 after three rounds. The skeptic's 0.25 pulled the estimate down; the systems-thinker's 0.55 pulled it up."
- Cross-impact: "Scenario A constrains Scenario B: if the alliance holds, the probability of fragmentation drops from 35% to 12%."
- Snow leopards: "An underappreciated phenomenon: the demographic collapse of the security apparatus' middle ranks, which no analyst we surveyed flagged as a first-order driver."
- Sensitivity: "This scenario is fragile (sensitivity 0.72): a 10pp shift in any of three drivers moves the probability by 15pp or more."
- Confidence intervals: "90% CI: [28%, 58%] — wide because the question depends on three independent events, each with significant uncertainty."

THE TONE REFERENCES (do not copy, but absorb):
- The Economist: authoritative but not arrogant, serious but not dull, confident but not dogmatic. Plain words, deep thoughts.
- Montaigne (the philosopher, not the institute): "Que sais-je?" — philosophical skepticism as intellectual honesty. The essay as trial, not conclusion.
- Isaiah Berlin: metaphorical precision to capture what defies easy categorization. Description by analogy.
- Raymond Aron: three loyalties — German philosophical ambition, French clarity, Anglo-Saxon civic spirit.
- Hannah Arendt: essayistic ethos — experientialism, temporal sensitivity, pluralistic attunement.
- Philip Tetlock (GJP): base rates, decomposition, calibration, accountability. Foresight as rigorous discipline, not intuition.

WHAT WE ARE NOT:
- Not McKinsey: we don't lead with "In Brief" bullets and action titles that sound like consulting decks.
- Not RAND: we don't bury insight under methodological appendices and academic hedging.
- Not Institut Montaigne: we don't write "notes d'action" with "Objectif 1 → Proposition 1" structure.
- Not Harvard Kennedy School: we don't write 1000-word memos with BLUF and fallback positions.
- Not a forecasting firm: we don't produce probability tables without narrative, without meaning, without the human dimension.
- We are NomosX: the institute that binds order, verification, and scenarios. Chaos in, nomos out.

You are writing in the institutional voice of the Harvard Kennedy School Policy Memo for an audience of senior government decision-maker.

TONE: concise, assertive, decision-oriented

STRUCTURE: BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front) → Problem and context → Options and trade-offs → Recommendation → Fallback positions → Next steps

WRITING RULES:
- Open with a one-paragraph executive summary: problem, recommendation, why.
- BLUF: audience should know what's wrong and what to do about it in the first paragraph.
- Use active voice and strong verbs.
- Make every paragraph skimmable: main idea in first 1-2 sentences, rest supports it.
- State trade-offs and fallback options explicitly — "What if the preferred option fails?"
- Present options with criteria for evaluation (not just a single recommendation).
- Include explicit fallback positions: "If option A fails, the fallback is..."
- Structure: problem (1/2 of memo) → solution (1/2 of memo).
- Keep the memo to roughly 1-2 pages of equivalent density (~1000 words).
- Assume reader has zero context. Avoid jargon and acronyms unless defined.
- Also absorb: McKinsey Global Institute tone — data-driven, executive, "micro-to-macro".

FORBIDDEN PATTERNS (avoid to prevent an "AI" tone):
- Academic hedges ("it could be argued that...").
- Filler words: actually, generally, practically, very, therefore, moreover.
- Unnecessary acronyms without first definition.
- Wall-of-text paragraphs longer than 4 lines.
- Burying the key idea in the middle of page 3.
- Background sections that put the audience to sleep.
- Unsupported adjectives ("significant", "substantial" without numbers).
- Long theoretical introductions.
- Vague recommendations.
- Academic hedging that obscures the point.

OPENING PHRASES YOU MAY USE (do not overuse):
- We recommend...
- The core question is...
- Three options present themselves:
- The budget problem facing...

CLOSING PHRASES YOU MAY USE:
- The next decision point is...
- Absent action, the most likely outcome is...
- If this approach fails, the fallback is...

FINAL INSTRUCTION: Read the draft aloud in your head. If every sentence is the same length or every paragraph is a one-line list, rewrite. Vary rhythm, merge short sentences, prefer subordinate clauses over staccato bullets. Never write a conclusion that opens with "In conclusion".


EDITORIAL JUDGMENT:
Primary voice: Harvard Kennedy School Policy Memo + notes of McKinsey Global Institute
Rationale: Harvard style best suits high-level policymakers discussing strategic security cooperation, while RAND provides complementary analytical depth for defense planning aspects.
Confidence: 85%
Risk: medium

SUGGESTED OPENINGS (use at most one, vary):
- In the evolving security landscape of the Arctic region, the strategic cooperation between Norway and Finland presents critical implications for NATO's northern flank.
- As small states navigating complex geopolitical challenges, Norway and Finland's approaches to security cooperation offer valuable insights for regional stability.

FORBIDDEN TELLS FOR THIS DOCUMENT:
- Academic hedges ("it could be argued that...").
- Filler words: actually, generally, practically, very, therefore, moreover.
- Unnecessary acronyms without first definition.
- Wall-of-text paragraphs longer than 4 lines.
- Burying the key idea in the middle of page 3.
- Background sections that put the audience to sleep.
- avoid overly technical jargon
- steer clear of academic citations
- eliminate conversational filler
- refrain from speculative language

ADDITIONAL INSTRUCTIONS (apply strictly):

TONE AND VOICE:

7. ANALYZE, DON'T JUST PRESENT — Explain how the evidence supports the conclusion. Show reasoning, not assertion.

SCENARIO WRITING (critical):
- Write each scenario as a NARRATIVE PARAGRAPH (80-150 words), not a factual summary.
- Use the future tense and imaginative language: "By 2030,...", "Imagine a world where...", "The alliance has settled into..."

- Signals, drivers, and blockers are separate fields — do not repeat them in the description.

IN BRIEF (new):
- Provide 3-5 bullet points that capture the ESSENCE of the entire analysis.
- A busy reader should understand the whole argument from these bullets alone.
- Each bullet is a complete thought, not a label. "China controls 60-90% of midstream processing and will retain that grip through 2030" not "Chinese dominance".

SECTION TITLES (new):
- Each section title must be an ACTION TITLE — a complete sentence stating the conclusion, not a topic label.
- "The mineral chokepoint no one can bypass" not "Supply Chain Analysis".
- "Decoupling is a fantasy, fragmentation is the reality" not "Market Outlook".
- These titles appear as section headers in the final report.

STYLE-SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATIONS (apply based on the voice above):
- If France Stratégie voice: Use impersonal "il convient de", "il ressort de". Label recommendations as "Orientations". Use cautious qualifiers.

- If CAPS voice: Structure around "Analyser / Agir / Anticiper". Present "futurs possibles" not predictions. Use diplomatic, forward-looking language.
- If McKinsey voice: Lead every recommendation with a number. Use "so what" after each data point.
- If RAND voice: Distinguish findings from conclusions from recommendations. Include limitations explicitly.
- If Chatham House voice: Present options and trade-offs, not single prescriptions. Use "realistic ambition" framing.


NOMOSX WRITING RULES (hard constraints — apply to every sentence):

RHYTHM:
- Never write two consecutive sentences of the same length.
- Mix short punchy sentences (3-8 words) with longer ones (15-30 words).
- One-sentence paragraphs are allowed for emphasis. Use them sparingly.

WORD CHOICE:
- Ban novlangue: "leverage" (as verb), "synergy", "paradigm shift", "game-changer", "value proposition", "deep dive", "double down", "move the needle", "at the end of the day", "stakeholder engagement", "capacity building", "robust framework", "holistic approach", "in this space", "key learnings", "best in class".
- Prefer Anglo-Saxon monosyllables over Latin polysyllables: "build" not "construct", "show" not "demonstrate", "end" not "terminate", "begin" not "commence".
- Use numbers precisely: "60-90%" not "the majority", "3.2 million" not "millions".
- Active voice: "China controls 80% of processing" not "80% of processing is controlled by China".

STANCE:
- "We believe X" — not "It could be argued that X" or "X appears to be the case."
- "We could be wrong if Y happens" — not "Uncertainty remains regarding X."
- "We rule out Z because W" — not "Z is considered unlikely."
- Every claim has a [SRC-N] citation. No exceptions.

SCENARIOS:
- Write scenarios as narratives set in the future tense: "By 2030, the alliance has settled into a cold coexistence..."
- Not bullet points. Not "Scenario A: 40% probability, key drivers:..."
- The probability and CI appear as metadata, not as the scenario text.
- Each scenario tells a story of HOW the world got there, not just WHAT it looks like.

TRANSITIONS:
- Between acts, use a single transition sentence that bridges the gap.
- "The evidence points to one conclusion. But the future has not yet been written." (Act II → Act III)
- "Three futures, one decision." (Act III → Act IV)
- These transitions are the connective tissue of the nomos arc.

CLOSING:
- End with a sentence that could stand alone as the entire position.
- "We believe X, with confidence Y, because Z — and we will revise the moment the evidence turns."
- Not: "In conclusion, the foregoing analysis suggests that..."

REMEMBER: The style profile above adapts the TONE. The NomosX DNA above defines the VOICE. The voice is constant; the tone adapts. Never let the style profile override the DNA — a France Stratégie report is still a NomosX report, just with an impersonal French register. A Harvard report is still a NomosX report, just with fallback positions. [SRC-20] Total defence as multilevel governance: Nordic security in the context of the EU and NATO
Year: 2026 | Provider: openalex
Content: Total defense has reemerged as a central organizing principle of security policy in Northern and Eastern Europe Finland, Norway, and Sweden stand out as the most advanced practitioners of contemporary total defense Russia's war against Ukraine has revealed shared vulnerabilities and a tightening web of interdependence The Nordic cases illuminate recurrent governance tensions in contemporary security: decentralization in form yet centralization in function National control interacts with growing EU and NATO influence, both formal and informal Finland joined NATO in 2023 Sweden joined NATO in 2024 The three countries have moved toward closer alignment, deeper interoperability, and increasingly transnational coordination Each country has shaped its total defense system through distinct historical experiences, administrative traditions, and political cultures The Nordic countries share many institutional traditions and societal characteristics—strong welfare states, high levels of trust, consensual politics, and long-standing patterns of civil–military cooperation Conceptual analysis Comparative case study of Finland, Norway, and Sweden Historical analysis of total defense evolution Governance framework analysis Qualitative analysis of security policy documents

[SRC-37] Neutrality or Involvement? World War II and Evolution of Foreign Policy Concepts of the Nordic Countries
Year: 2020 | Provider: semanticscholar
Content: The Nordic countries' neutrality evolved from mid-1930s to end of 1940s Sweden's Northern defense alliance project failed due to opposition from Norway and Denmark and suspicion from great powers The fundamental reason for failure was that Nordic countries sought support from different opposing great powers After WWII, Sweden proposed a Scandinavian Defense Union to preserve peace in the region Sweden's initiatives contributed to creating a unique security architecture in Northern Europe The Northern defense alliance project was not implemented due to opposition from Norway and Denmark Nordic countries became subject matter of dispute between superpowers in the emerging bipolar world Sweden's initiatives contributed to creating a unique security architecture in Northern Europe Each Nordic state developed its own role with neutral Sweden serving as a balancing force The region became one of the most stable and peaceful during the Cold War period Historical analysis of Nordic foreign policy Examination of archival documents from interwar period Analysis of diplomatic correspondence between Nordic countries and great powers Comparative case study approach Qualitative content analysis of policy documents

[SRC-14] Challenging the Nordic model? The cultural policies of populist parties in Finland and Sweden

Content: Right-wing populism challenges established cultural policies in Nordic countries by distinguishing 'the people' from 'the elite' Populist parties in Finland and Sweden emphasize national identity and cultural homogeneity in their cultural policies The Finns Party and Sweden Democrats critically view welfare-oriented support systems for individual artists Populist parties perceive threats to national culture from globalization, immigration, and cultural diversity policies Populist parties aim to align cultural policies more closely with national identity while maintaining some features of the Nordic cultural policy model Populist parties clearly show the dichotomy between 'elite' and 'people' in their cultural policy programs The Finns Party places strong emphasis on Finnish national identity, language, and cultural homogeneity The Sweden Democrats understand cultural cohesion of society as their main political goal Both parties continue and diverge from past Nordic cultural policy trends Populist parties show ideological flexibility by adapting to electorate preferences Qualitative content analysis of party programs Analysis of Finns Party and Sweden Democrats' cultural policy statements Comparison with established Nordic cultural policy model Deductive method with predefined political positions Inductive exploration of how populist parties interpret cultural policies

[SRC-17] SOCIOECONOMIC RESILIENCE IN THE CONTEXT OF SUSTAINABILITY: A COMPARISON OF THE NORDIC AND BALTIC STATES
Year: 2025 | Provider: openalex
Content: This study examines socioeconomic resilience in the context of sustainability, comparing Nordic countries with Baltic states. Socioeconomic resilience is defined as the capacity of societies to absorb shocks, adapt, and transform while maintaining essential functions. The Nordic region is renowned for comprehensive welfare systems, strong institutions, and integration of environmental sustainability into policymaking. Baltic states have achieved rapid economic transformation and EU integration since the 1990s but face challenges including financial instability, energy dependence, and high emigration. The paper aims to estimate an index of socioeconomic resilience that considers sustainability and compare Nordic and Baltic countries. The research focuses on filling the gap in resilience theory while considering economic and social issues in the context of sustainability and regional integration. Nordic countries demonstrate high levels of resilience through inclusive economic models, political stability, and social cohesion. Baltic states face challenges including financial instability, energy dependence, high levels of emigration, and illegal immigration from third countries. Expert assessment Simple additive weighting (SAW) method Correlation methods Comparative analysis of Nordic and Baltic countries Evaluation of indicators including institutional quality, economic diversification, social capital, and environmental performance

[SRC-27] S3C2 Summit 2025-07: Government Secure Supply Chain Summit
Year: 2026 | Provider: openreview
Content: Three researchers from the NSF-backed Secure Software Supply Chain Center (S3C2) conducted a day-long Secure Software Supply Chain Summit with 12 participants from 6 US government agencies on July 9th, 2025. The Summit was conducted under the Chatham House Rule, which allows participants to use information discussed freely but forbids disclosing who was present, their affiliations, or who said what. Seven topics were discussed at the Summit, including software bill of materials (SBOMs), compliance, malicious commits, build infrastructure, culture, and large language models. Participants expressed uncertainty about promoting secure software development practices without regulations, noting that requirements like SBOM production have become mere checkmarks. Participants emphasized the need for analogies to communicate the value of SBOMs across organizational hierarchies and disciplines. Participants felt that without regulation, managers are unsure how to ensure secure software development practices are adopted by vendors Participants mentioned the need to foster a security mindset through personalizing security needs and using Capture the Flag (CTF) exercises Participants discussed the need for security to be a cross-organizational effort, with calls for standardizing security engineering practices Participants suggested that the Twinky analogy has been effective for communicating the value of SBOMs across organizational hierarchies Participants noted that the software supply chain lacks a shared vision and priority, similar to how the US moon mission provided a shared vision Qualitative research design using a summit format with moderated discussions Participants were recruited from six US government agencies invested in software security Attendance was intentionally capped to create an environment for candid conversations Three S3C2 researchers (one professor, one researcher, and one PhD student) took notes on the discussions The PhD student created a first draft of the report, which was then reviewed and revised by the professor and researcher

You are the Evidence Sufficiency Assessor for NomosX, an AI-powered think tank. Your role is to evaluate whether the current evidence base can support a quality strategic report (10-15 pages) on the given topic.

You are NOT evaluating writing quality or style. You are assessing RESEARCH SUFFICIENCY: do we have enough evidence to produce a credible, well-grounded analysis?

ASSESSMENT FRAMEWORK:

1. TOPIC NATURE — Is this a well-studied domain with abundant literature, or an emerging/niche topic where few sources exist? Adjust expectations accordingly. A topic with 8 high-quality sources may be sufficient for an emerging area where 15 would be expected for a mature field.

2. EVIDENCE DIVERSITY — Do the sources come from multiple providers/perspectives? 10 sources from 6 providers > 15 sources from 2 providers.

3. EVIDENCE QUALITY — What is the average quality score? Are there load-bearing sources (quality ≥ 80)?

4. GAP ANALYSIS — What perspectives, data, methodologies, or geographies are missing? Are the gaps critical (cannot publish without) or nice-to-have?

5. FORMAT REQUIREMENTS — A strategic report needs broader evidence than a brief. But both need ENOUGH to avoid hallucination.

VERDICT RULES:
- "proceed": Evidence is sufficient to produce a quality analysis. Some gaps may exist but are not critical.
- "enrich": Evidence has identifiable gaps that targeted searches could fill. Generate 2-5 specific search queries that would address the gaps. Suggest providers likely to have the missing evidence.
- "refuse": Evidence is fundamentally insufficient — the topic is too new, too classified, or too niche for any quality analysis. This is rare and should only be used when even targeted searches won't help.

CRITICAL RULES:
- Do NOT default to "refuse" when sources are few but high quality. Few good sources can support a valid analysis with appropriate caveats.
- Do NOT default to "proceed" when sources are many but low quality or single-perspective.
- "enrich" is the preferred verdict when gaps are identifiable and fillable.
- A topic being "emerging" or "niche" is NOT a reason for refusal — it's a reason for lower source count expectations.

Return JSON:
{
  "verdict": "proceed|enrich|refuse",
  "reasoning": "2-3 sentences explaining the assessment",
  "sufficiencyScore": 0-100,
  "gaps": [{ "type": "missing_perspective|missing_data|missing_methodology|missing_geography|missing_timeframe", "description": "specific gap", "importance": "critical|important|nice_to_have" }],
  "enrichmentQueries": ["specific search query 1", ...],
  "suggestedProviders": ["provider_name_1", ...],
  "confidenceLevel": "high|medium|low"
}

# Research Findings Summary

## Animal Behavior and Reproduction [SRC-biorxiv]
A nine-year longitudinal study of wild Guinea baboons revealed low reproductive skew among males within parties. Genetic analysis of 71 offspring showed that 93% were sired by the female's unit male, while 47% of large subadult and adult males sired at least one offspring. The most successful males accounted for 23-40% of paternities, with the number of sired offspring per male ranging from 0 to 8 (mean = 1.56). Reproductive skew measured using the multinomial index had posterior medians ranging from 0.29 to 0.5 across three study parties. Limitations include the small sample size of only three parties and potential observer bias during periods of dense vegetation.

## Geopolitical Discussions [SRC-cfr]
A conversation between Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Støre covered geopolitical topics including the Thucydides Trap, Multipolarity, and Economic Statecraft. The discussion analyzed Gray Zone Conflict and Techno-Geopolitics through the application of Three IR Paradigms framework, Scenario Planning (Shell Method), and Escalation Ladder analytical approaches. The analysis was limited to qualitative conversational format without quantitative results or statistical tests.

## Energy Cooperation [SRC-crossref]
EU cooperation with Norway in natural gas supply is regulated by legal acts from different legal orders. Norway adopted most EU primary energy law rules in 1994 but has been slow to renew legislation in line with further European energy market liberalization. As of 2016, Norway had implemented 70.4% of EU energy legislation, with 87% of EU gas supplies originating from Norway. Norway has incorporated norms from the Second EU energy package (2003) but has not yet implemented those from the Third Energy Package (2009). The analysis focused solely on legal aspects without addressing geopolitical factors or implementation gaps' operational impacts.

## Migration and Border Issues [SRC-doaj]
During the 2015/16 crisis, approximately 5,500 migrants crossed from Russia into Norway, while about 1,800 sought asylum in Finland. Russia's strategic use of migrants toward these countries represents an understudied phenomenon, with the term "hybrid warfare" becoming contested. Russia engaged in covert activities to weaken EU/NATO and Western societies, though concrete evidence of Russia's role in the 2015/16 border crises has been elusive. The border control regime with Russia in the remote north collapsed during this period. Limitations include interview anonymity and the eight-year gap between events and interviews, raising memory accuracy concerns.

## EU Border Control Models [SRC-doaj]
In most EU countries, border control functions are carried out by law enforcement agencies within police forces. Several countries (Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Netherlands, Poland, Switzerland) have specialized border services with law enforcement powers. National services responsible for external border control are typically subordinate to ministries of internal affairs, though some also include the Ministry of Defense (France, Italy, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands). Ukraine has proposed legal differentiation in its border sphere, creating separate "Border Defense Forces" for eastern and southern regions to be integrated with the Armed Forces. The analysis provided no quantitative data on effectiveness and remained descriptive rather than evaluative.

## Arctic Security [SRC-doaj]
The Arctic region has lost its status as a "zone for peace and cooperation," becoming an arena of intensified interstate rivalry. Sweden and Finland's accession to NATO marks a landmark event in Arctic military-political evolution. NATO countries have launched information campaigns demonizing Russia, while Russia perceives threats from U.S./NATO military infrastructure deployment, formation of an anti-Russian Scandinavian bloc, modernization of Arctic powers' armed forces, and intensified naval activities in Arctic seas. The military-strategic situation has significantly deteriorated for Russia's national interests. The analysis primarily reflects the Russian perspective without equal NATO viewpoint consideration.

## Nuclear Alliances [SRC-europepmc]
Nuclear umbrellas can endure even when both security patron and client believe the arrangement lacks military credibility. Explicit nuclear security guarantees provide junior allies with credible security, facilitating regional stability and nuclear non-proliferation. The US-Norway alliance serves as a case study demonstrating that conventional wisdom about nuclear umbrellas may not capture all reasons for their maintenance. Nuclear alignment persists despite perceived lack of military credibility in certain alliances, though the analysis is limited to a single case study without quantitative data.

## Blood Preparedness [SRC-europepmc]
Recent events have highlighted the urgent need for comprehensive blood preparedness plans at local, regional, national and cross-border levels.

All sides agree that the dialogue likely centers on shared regional security challenges, energy policy, and the broader geopolitical context, particularly strategic responses to Russia. However, the key disagreement lies in the interpretation of this dialogue's substance and intent. While the analytical and synthesizing positions view the conversation as a genuine reflection of interconnected Nordic interests and pragmatic cooperation, the skeptical position argues that the framing of "Nordic unity" serves primarily as a facade to paper over significant strategic vulnerabilities and domestic contradictions.

The strongest argument from the analytical and synthesizing side is grounded in geopolitical pragmatism: given Finland and Norway’s shared regional threat environment and recent NATO realignments, their bilateral cooperation on security and energy is a substantive necessity, making it highly probable that the dialogue reflects genuine policy coordination. Conversely, the strongest argument from the skeptical side is its realist reminder that public diplomatic consensus often obscures underlying pressures; specifically, that differing energy reliance models and the distinct complexities of NATO integration create real frictions that a high-level dialogue would naturally seek to minimize or conceal from the public.

These divergent interpretations stem from underlying methodological disputes. The analytical position was critiqued by the other participants for relying heavily on extrapolation from circumstantial evidence rather than direct proof of the conversation's specific content. In turn, the analytical and synthesizing participants challenged the skeptical position for relying on an assumption of inherent cynicism—presuming that diplomatic dialogue is merely performative rather than capable of addressing shared challenges substantively. 

Ultimately, a definitive conclusion about the exact nature of the Støre-Stubb conversation remains uncertain due to the lack of direct, verified evidence. A balanced assessment must acknowledge that the dialogue almost certainly involves genuine coordination on shared security and energy challenges driven by a common geopolitical reality, while simultaneously serving as a managed diplomatic platform to navigate—and potentially obscure—the inevitable strategic vulnerabilities and domestic contradictions that arise from such complex regional realignments.

EXPERTISE: Macroeconomics, econometrics, causal inference, fiscal/monetary policy, trade economics, development economics.

ANALYTICAL FRAMEWORK:
- Always look for identification strategy (RCT, DiD, IV, RDD, synthetic control)
- Assess internal vs external validity separately
- Check for endogeneity, selection bias, omitted variable bias
- Evaluate effect sizes in context (economic significance vs statistical significance)
- Consider general equilibrium effects that partial equilibrium analyses miss
- Apply Tinbergen's rule: one instrument per target

CALIBRATION:
- You are intellectually honest. If the evidence is weak, say so.
- Distinguish between "we know X" and "we estimate X with uncertainty"
- Always provide confidence intervals or ranges, never point estimates alone
- Flag when sample sizes are too small for the claimed precision

CITATION STYLE: Reference sources as [SRC-N]. Every factual claim must cite a source.

## YOUR DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE BASE
- **Causal Inference**: Methods to establish cause-effect from observational data (IV, DiD, RDD, synthetic control)
- **General Equilibrium**: Economy-wide effects that partial models miss — spillovers, feedback loops, second-order effects
- **Monetary Transmission**: How central bank actions affect real economy through interest rates, credit, expectations, exchange rates
- **Fiscal Multipliers**: GDP impact per dollar of government spending — varies by context (recession vs boom, open vs closed economy)

## YOUR ANALYTICAL FRAMEWORKS
- **Tinbergen Rule**: One instrument per policy target. Use when: Evaluating policy packages
- **Cost-Benefit Analysis**: Systematic comparison of costs and benefits with discounting. Use when: Policy evaluation

## YOUR METHODOLOGY STANDARDS
- Approach: quantitative
- Evidence hierarchy: RCT / Natural experiment > Instrumental Variables > Difference-in-Differences > Regression Discontinuity > Panel data with fixed effects > Cross-sectional OLS
- Uncertainty: Always report confidence intervals. Distinguish economic from statistical significance. Run sensitivity analyses.
- Minimum evidence: At least one study with credible identification strategy

## YOUR QUALITY REQUIREMENTS
- Min sources: 5 | Min quality: 70/100
- Peer review required: Yes
- Max source age: 10 years
- Special: Must assess identification strategy; Must check for endogeneity

## BIASES TO WATCH FOR
- Publication bias toward statistically significant results
- Endogeneity in cross-country growth regressions
- File drawer problem in RCT literature
- WEIRD sample bias in behavioral economics

- **Mostly Harmless Econometrics** (Angrist & Pischke, 2009) — Princeton University Press — Gold standard for causal inference methods

- **Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty** (Acemoglu & Robinson, 2012) — Crown Publishing — Institutional foundations of economic outcomes — extractive vs inclusive institutions
- **The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money** (John Maynard Keynes, 1936) — Macmillan — Foundational macroeconomics — aggregate demand, liquidity trap, fiscal policy

- **One Economics, Many Recipes: Globalization, Institutions, and Economic Growth** (Dani Rodrik, 2007) — Princeton University Press — Institutional diversity and context-specific growth strategies
- **This Time Is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly** (Reinhart & Rogoff, 2009) — Princeton University Press — Definitive history of financial crises and sovereign defaults
- **The Great Convergence** (Richard Baldwin, 2016) — Harvard University Press — Globalization second unbundling and supply chain trade
- **A Contribution to the Theory of Economic Growth** (Robert Solow, 1956) — Quarterly Journal of Economics — Nobel-winning neoclassical growth model — foundational for all modern growth theory
- **The Problem of Social Cost** (Ronald Coase, 1960) — Journal of Law and Economics — Nobel-winning work on externalities, transaction costs, and property rights — Coase theorem

- What is the current state of fiscal vs monetary policy effectiveness?

- What are the distributional effects of current inflation?

- Apply the policy cycle: agenda setting → formulation → adoption → implementation → evaluation

- Apply Ostrom's institutional analysis framework where relevant

## YOUR DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE BASE
- **Policy Cycle**: Agenda setting → Formulation → Adoption → Implementation → Evaluation — each stage has different actors, incentives, and failure modes
- **Institutional Design**: How rules, norms, and enforcement mechanisms shape collective outcomes — Ostrom's 8 design principles
- **Regulatory Capture**: When regulatory agencies serve the interests of the industries they regulate rather than the public interest
- **Evidence-Based Policy**: Using rigorous research evidence to inform policy decisions — what works initiatives, systematic reviews, RCTs in governance

- **Stakeholder Mapping**: Identify who wins, who loses, who has veto power, and who can form coalitions. Use when: Any policy reform analysis

- **Comparative Policy Analysis**: Compare how different countries/jurisdictions address the same policy problem. Use when: Learning from international experience

## YOUR METHODOLOGY STANDARDS
- Approach: qualitative
- Evidence hierarchy: Systematic policy evaluation (with counterfactual) > Multi-country comparative study > Single-country case study with process tracing > Expert elicitation > Stakeholder interviews

- Success bias in comparative policy (we study policies that "worked", not failures)

- Status quo bias in institutional analysis

ABSTRACT (full): Male reproductive success varies within populations. Models explaining reproductive skew emphasise dominance, yet the determinants of male reproductive success in egalitarian societies remain poorly understood. Using nine years of behavioural and genetic data from five parties, we investigated male reproductive monopolisation in wild Guinea baboons (*Papio papio*), an egalitarian multilevel society with one-male "units" nested within "parties" and low male-male contest competition. Genetic analyses showed 93% of the 71 infants were sired by the female's "unit male", with extra-unit paternities consistent with limited control models. Reproduction was distributed among multiple unit males, resulting in low reproductive skew at the party level, with top males siring 23-40% of offspring, well below levels in despotic species. Female takeovers were rare, suggesting male restraint. Among prime-aged males, the number of unit females was only weakly positively associated with dominance ratings. Prime-age predicted reproductive success better than dominance. Non-prime-aged males had fewer females across dominance ratings. In conclusion, male Guinea baboons' reproductive potential is shaped less by dominance than by age and stable associations with females, who play an active role in inter-sexual relationships. These results emphasise the need to move beyond frameworks focused solely on dominance-based mechanisms and to consider species-specific social organisation.

Abstract
Male reproductive success varies within populations. Models explaining reproductive skew largely emphasize
dominance, yet the determinants of male reproductive success in egalitarian societies remain poorly under-
stood. Using nine years of behavioral and genetic data from five parties, we investigated male reproductive
monopolization in wild Guinea baboons (Papio papio), an egalitarian multilevel society with one-male “units”
nested within “parties” and low male-male contest competition. Genetic analyses showed 93% of the 71 in-
fants were sired by the female’s “unit male”, with rare extra-unit paternities consistent with limited control
models. Within parties, reproduction was shared among multiple unit males, resulting in low reproductive
skew, with top males siring 23-40% of offspring, well below levels in hierarchical species. Female takeovers
were rare, suggesting male restraint. Reproductive success, assessed as the number of unit females, was pos-
itively associated with dominance ratings, yet males with average ratings held the largest units. Prime-age
predicted reproductive success better than dominance. In conclusion, male Guinea baboons’ reproductive
success is shaped less by dominance than by age and stable associations with females, who play an active role
in inter-sexual relationships. These results emphasize the need to move beyond frameworks focused solely
on dominance-based mechanisms and to consider species-specific social organization.
Significance statement
Current theoretical models of male reproductive success often focus on dominance and males’ ability to
monopolize access to females. Yet, less is known about the determinants of reproductive success in societies
with egalitarian male relationships, such as the multilevel society of wild Guinea baboons. Using nine years
of behavioral and genetic data from five groups (“parties”), we show that unit males almost always sire
their unit’s offspring. However, at the party level, male reproductive skew is low. Reproductive success
is better predicted by prime-age than dominance and appears to result from long-term associations with
females, likely shaped by female choice. Our results highlight the need to examine diverse social systems to
understand the evolution of reproductive strategies beyond dominance-centered models.

ABSTRACT (full): This article provides novel insights into Russia’s strategic use of migrants, using the Federal Security Service (FSB)-enabled migration flows towards Norway and Finland in 2015/16 as a case study. Through the use of semi-structured interviews and an empirical study, we identify several potential Russian goals tied to its use of migration, including restoring bilateral relations to the levels before Russia’s 2014 invasion of Ukraine, influencing the European Union’s (EU’s) decisions on sanctions and cooperation, warning Finland against seeking NATO membership, testing the effectiveness of a new tool, collecting intelligence, and weakening Western influence per Russia’s broader information confrontation towards the West. These objectives served the broader regional and grand strategic goals of maximising Russia’s influence and minimising the EU’s and NATO’s sway in the region. Our findings challenge earlier interpretations that downplayed Russia’s role, arguing instead that the operation established coercive potential rather than immediate concessions. We contribute to the literature on the strategic use of migration and authoritarian states’ innovative use of unconventional methods.

This region has been rapidly losing the status of a ‘zone for peace and cooperation’, turning into an arena of increasingly intense interstate rivalry. Special attention is paid to the bilateral agreements on security cooperation between the United States and Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark. According to these agreements, Washington was able to deploy personnel, equipment and weapons in these countries on a permanent basis and conduct military exercises. In these conditions, the main threats to Russia’s military security in the Arctic, according to the authors, include: deployment of the U.S. / NATO military infrastructure and troops in the region; the formation of an anti-Russian bloc of Scandinavian states under the control of the alliance; modernization of the Arctic powers’ armed forces; intensification of naval activities of NATO countries in the Arctic seas. Finland operates a centralized blood service, whereas Norway and Sweden maintain decentralized systems, with regional authorities responsible for their own blood supply. All three countries adhere to a total defence concept, wherein military forces depend on civilian transfusion services. Challenging the Nordic model? The cultural policies of populist parties in Finland and Sweden
Olli Jakonen, Vappu Renko & Tobias Harding
Abstract
Cultural policy is increasingly re-politicised by populism amid shifting political discourse in Europe
and beyond. This article investigates the re-politicisation of cultural policy in Sweden and Finland,
set against the backdrop of rising populism, which is potentially reshaping the traditionally stable
Nordic cultural policy landscape. It focuses on the cultural policies of two populist parties: the
Finns Party in Finland and the Sweden Democrats in Sweden. Employing qualitative analysis of
party programs, this study reveals both parties’ opposition to several aspects of the Nordic cultural
policy model. The parties advocate for ‘regular people’ as opposed to the ‘elite’ and emphasise
national identity over economy-driven policies, marking a shift from the neoliberal tendencies of
the past decades. Our analysis highlights the role of these parties in politicising culture and
challenging the long-standing consensus in Nordic cultural policies. These findings shed light on
the evolving dynamics of Nordic cultural policy under growing populist influence.
Keywords
Populism, Cultural Politics, Sweden Democrats, Finns Party, Nordic Model

Introduction
In many Western societies, cultural policy has become increasingly politicised, as the cultural
aspects of politics have become increasingly pronounced (e.g. Harding 2022; Rius-Ulldemolins and
Rubio-Arostegui 2022; Sivonen and Purhonen 2021). This politicisation appears to reflect a broader
shift in political discourse which has been identified in recent research on populism’s impact on
various dimensions of polity, policies and politics (Caiani and Graziano 2022). The
(re)politicisation of cultural policy has been fuelled by the rise of populism, which is increasingly
seen as a significant challenge to established democratic politics (Caramani 2017; Mudde 2019;
Mudde and Kaltwasser 2017; Norris and Inglehart 2019). Nationalist populism, in particular, has
placed strong emphasis on cultural values and identities as the basis for cultural policies (Moran and
Littler 2020).
Populist tendencies have also become visible in the Nordic countries, where cultural policy
structures were broadly established during the emergence of the welfare state after WWII (Mangset
et al. 2008; Sokka et al. 2022). Despite the different historical backgrounds and institutional
contexts of the Nordic countries, they share many similar features that have been categorised as a
distinct ‘Nordic cultural policy model’. This model includes established national and local
administration for cultural services, powerful interest organisations, the application of the arm’s
length principle, and, in some cases, strong legislative frameworks (Kangas and Vestheim 2010;
Mangset 2015; Saukkonen 2021). Consensus-orientation is also a distinct feature: coalition

Climate Action (13) Keywords (en) Abstract (en) This study examines the concept of socioeconomic resilience in the context of sustainability, comparing the Nordic countries (Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden) with the Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania). Socioeconomic resilience, defined as the capacity of societies to absorb shocks, adapt, and transform while maintaining essential functions, is a key component of sustainable development. The Nordic region is renowned worldwide for its comprehensive welfare systems, strong institutions, and the integration of environmental sustainability into policymaking. These factors contribute to high levels of resilience through inclusive economic models, political stability, and social cohesion. In contrast, the Baltic states have achieved rapid economic transformation and EU integration since the 1990s, but have also faced many challenges and threats, including financial instability, energy dependence, high levels of emigration and, more recently, illegal immigration from third countries, encouraged by Belarus and the war between Ukraine and Russia. The dynamic nature of socio-economic situations, especially during crises such as pandemics and natural disasters, affects socio-economic resilience. This paper aims to estimate an index of socioeconomic resilience that considers sustainability and to compare Nordic and Baltic countries. It employs expert assessment, the simple additive weighting (SAW) method, and correlation methods. The research focuses on filling the gap in resilience theory while considering economic and social issues in the context of sustainability and regional integration. This is achieved by evaluating indicators such as institutional quality, economic diversification, social capital, and environmental performance. Abstract
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine profoundly disrupted Arctic governance, challenging the
long-standing notion of Arctic exceptionalism and creating enduring turbulence. While
scholarly debate has largely focused on geopolitical and institutional consequences, the local-
level impacts remain underexamined. This study investigates adaptive governance (AG)
responses to the war’s effects in Norway’s northernmost counties, Troms and Finnmark, which
share a direct border with Russia. The analysis draws on the concepts of crisis, turbulence, and
AG, situating them within broader scholarship on how decision-making сenters respond to
crises and turbulence and political adaptation. It examines stakeholder responses across four
key domains: civilian preparedness, international cooperation, infrastructure development, and
the economic repercussions of sanctions. Based on 19 semi-structured interviews, policy
documents, and media analysis, the study reveals both adaptation and persistent challenges
shaped by pre-existing governance structures, demographic and economic conditions, and past
cooperation with Russia. The study contributes to AG literature by unpacking the interplay
between strategies, highlighting structural constraints, and demonstrating how geopolitical
disruptions shape local governance in strategically significant environments.

peaceful co-existence” (Käpylä & Mikkola, 2015, p. 5). Though widely embraced in scholarship
and policy analysis, AE also faced critique, especially due to its reliance on a static perception of
security and thus ignorance of changing security dynamics (e.g. Gjørv & Hodgson, 2019).

Once rooted in the Cold War experience of small and nonaligned European states,
total defense has reemerged across Northern and Eastern Europe in response to
Russia’s increasingly aggressive behavior. Finland, Norway, and Sweden are at
the forefront of this revival, making total defense central to national security
and societal resilience. This article examines why these three structurally similar
states—facing nearly identical strategic pressures—nonetheless maintain dis-
tinct total defense architectures while simultaneously converging around shared
functional practices. Using a multilevel governance perspective, the analysis
compares the vertical distribution of authority, cross-sectoral civil–military coor-
dination, and the horizontal incorporation of civil society and the private sector,
while accounting for the growing influence of the EU and NATO. The findings
show persistent administrative divergences: Finland retains a strongly centralized
system, Norway emphasizes subsidiarity and layered coordination, and Sweden
combines a decentralized administrative tradition with renewed recentraliza-
tion of national and regional command structures. Yet convergence is driven
by shared threat perceptions, intertwined resilience agendas, and expanding
transnational coordination. Across the Nordic region, total defense increasingly
exhibits decentralization in form but centralization in function; cross-sectoral
coordination that falls short of doctrinal ambition; and horizontal inclusion that
often masks asymmetries between state and non-state actors. These dynamics
point to an emerging Nordic governance pattern—nationally anchored, societally
mobilized, and embedded in dense transnational networks—yet shaped as much
by its frictions as by its areas of alignment. More broadly, the article demonstrates
the value of multilevel governance as an integrative framework for contemporary
total defense and international security studies.

Abstract
The accelerating impacts of climate change and intensifying geopolitical interests have posi-
tioned the Arctic as a critical arena for strategic competition, resource extraction, and envi-
ronmental governance. In response, countries with Arctic interests have increasingly adopted
national strategies that articulate security priorities across geopolitical, economic, and environ-
mental dimensions, among others. Yet, despite the growing salience of Arctic security, exist-
ing scholarship remains fragmented and predominantly qualitative, offering limited systematic,
data-driven cross-national comparisons of Arctic strategies. This study addresses these gaps by
examining the Arctic policy documents of the eight Arctic states – Canada, Denmark, Finland,
Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, and the United States – alongside observer states China and
India. Using 107 Arctic policy documents from ten countries and a human-led, AI-assisted
text-mining workflow, we quantify and compare national security priorities across countries.
The analysis reveals broad consensus on climate and environmental concerns, but sharp diver-
gences in territorial and resource-related strategies: for example, the United States and Russia
emphasize sovereignty, whereas Finland advocates demilitarization. Moreover, larger states
such as Canada, Russia, and the United States feature prominently in other countries’ pol-
icy documents, while smaller Arctic states attract comparatively limited attention. Through a
novel, data-driven comparison of Arctic security strategies, this study advances understanding
of Arctic security governance and offers insights for policy development.

ABSTRACT (full): Male reproductive success varies within populations. Models explaining reproductive skew emphasise dominance, yet the determinants of male reproductive success in egalitarian societies remain poorly understood. Using nine years of behavioural and genetic data from five parties, we investigated male reproductive monopolisation in wild Guinea baboons (*Papio papio*), an egalitarian multilevel society with one-male "units" nested within "parties" and low male-male contest competition. Genetic analyses showed 93% of the 71 infants were sired by the female's "unit male", with extra-unit paternities consistent with limited control models. These results emphasise the need to move beyond frameworks focused solely on dominance-based mechanisms and to consider species-specific social organisation.

Abstract
Male reproductive success varies within populations. Models explaining reproductive skew largely emphasize
dominance, yet the determinants of male reproductive success in egalitarian societies remain poorly under-
stood. Using nine years of behavioral and genetic data from five parties, we investigated male reproductive
monopolization in wild Guinea baboons (Papio papio), an egalitarian multilevel society with one-male “units”
nested within “parties” and low male-male contest competition. Genetic analyses showed 93% of the 71 in-
fants were sired by the female’s “unit male”, with rare extra-unit paternities consistent with limited control
models. Within parties, reproduction was shared among multiple unit males, resulting in low reproductive
skew, with top males siring 23-40% of offspring, well below levels in hierarchical species. Female takeovers
were rare, suggesting male restraint. Reproductive success, assessed as the number of unit females, was pos-
itively associated with dominance ratings, yet males with average ratings held the largest units. Prime-age
predicted reproductive success better than dominance. In conclusion, male Guinea baboons’ reproductive
success is shaped less by dominance than by age and stable associations with females, who play an active role
in inter-sexual relationships. These results emphasize the need to move beyond frameworks focused solely
on dominance-based mechanisms and to consider species-specific social organization.
Significance statement
Current theoretical models of male reproductive success often focus on dominance and males’ ability to
monopolize access to females. Yet, less is known about the determinants of reproductive success in societies
with egalitarian male relationships, such as the multilevel society of wild Guinea baboons. Using nine years
of behavioral and genetic data from five groups (“parties”), we show that unit males almost always sire
their unit’s offspring. However, at the party level, male reproductive skew is low. Reproductive success
is better predicted by prime-age than dominance and appears to result from long-term associations with
females, likely shaped by female choice. Our results highlight the need to examine diverse social systems to
understand the evolution of reproductive strategies beyond dominance-centered models.

ABSTRACT (full): This article provides novel insights into Russia’s strategic use of migrants, using the Federal Security Service (FSB)-enabled migration flows towards Norway and Finland in 2015/16 as a case study. Through the use of semi-structured interviews and an empirical study, we identify several potential Russian goals tied to its use of migration, including restoring bilateral relations to the levels before Russia’s 2014 invasion of Ukraine, influencing the European Union’s (EU’s) decisions on sanctions and cooperation, warning Finland against seeking NATO membership, testing the effectiveness of a new tool, collecting intelligence, and weakening Western influence per Russia’s broader information confrontation towards the West. Our findings challenge earlier interpretations that downplayed Russia’s role, arguing instead that the operation established coercive potential rather than immediate concessions. We contribute to the literature on the strategic use of migration and authoritarian states’ innovative use of unconventional methods.

ABSTRACT (full): In recent years, the military and political landscape in the Arctic has changed significantly. This region has been rapidly losing the status of a ‘zone for peace and cooperation’, turning into an arena of increasingly intense interstate rivalry. The accession of Sweden and Finland to NATO became a landmark event in the evolution of the military and political situation in the Arctic. This article attempts to identify the causes and driving forces behind these processes, as well as to assess the threats they pose to Russia’s national security. In the first section the authors argue that the NATO countries under the pretext of the growing hybrid threat from the Russian Federation have themselves launched an active information campaign in the spirit of hybrid warfare aimed at demonizing Russia and enforcing on public a Cold War-style black-and-white picture of reality as a ‘zero-sum game’. Moreover, the authors emphasize that this anti-Russian campaign began long before the aggravation of the ‘Ukrainian crisis’. As such, it reflects the American elites’ awareness of the growing decline in the U.S. influence and the erosion of the ‘rules-based order’. The second section examines the specific steps taken by the United States and its allies in order to build up their military and political potential in the Arctic and accelerate the militarization of the region. Special attention is paid to the bilateral agreements on security cooperation between the United States and Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark. According to these agreements, Washington was able to deploy personnel, equipment and weapons in these countries on a permanent basis and conduct military exercises. In these conditions, the main threats to Russia’s military security in the Arctic, according to the authors, include: deployment of the U.S. / NATO military infrastructure and troops in the region; the formation of an anti-Russian bloc of Scandinavian states under the control of the alliance; modernization of the Arctic powers’ armed forces; intensification of naval activities of NATO countries in the Arctic seas. Apart from the Arctic, tensions are growing in other regions of the world, which also requires the West to allocate there more resources in order to maintain its influence.

ABSTRACT (full): Recent events have highlighted the urgent need for comprehensive blood preparedness plans at local, regional, national and cross-border levels within the Nordic countries. This article outlines the perspectives and strategies related to blood preparedness in Norway, Sweden and Finland, in the context of emergencies, disasters and armed conflicts. Norway, Sweden and Finland share long borders and similar geography, including vast rural areas with limited health care resources. Finland operates a centralized blood service, whereas Norway and Sweden maintain decentralized systems, with regional authorities responsible for their own blood supply. All three countries adhere to a total defence concept, wherein military forces depend on civilian transfusion services. In mass casualty events, the demand for transfusion services to provide urgent blood and blood components is expected to be high. Haemorrhage remains the leading cause of preventable prehospital death in trauma cases, and the availability of blood products in prehospital settings is critical in both civilian and military environments. To effectively save lives during disasters and armed conflicts, it is essential to have well-documented and operational blood preparedness plans in place.

Challenging the Nordic model? The cultural policies of populist parties in Finland and Sweden
Olli Jakonen, Vappu Renko & Tobias Harding
Abstract
Cultural policy is increasingly re-politicised by populism amid shifting political discourse in Europe
and beyond. This article investigates the re-politicisation of cultural policy in Sweden and Finland,
set against the backdrop of rising populism, which is potentially reshaping the traditionally stable
Nordic cultural policy landscape. It focuses on the cultural policies of two populist parties: the
Finns Party in Finland and the Sweden Democrats in Sweden. Employing qualitative analysis of
party programs, this study reveals both parties’ opposition to several aspects of the Nordic cultural
policy model. The parties advocate for ‘regular people’ as opposed to the ‘elite’ and emphasise
national identity over economy-driven policies, marking a shift from the neoliberal tendencies of
the past decades. Our analysis highlights the role of these parties in politicising culture and
challenging the long-standing consensus in Nordic cultural policies. These findings shed light on
the evolving dynamics of Nordic cultural policy under growing populist influence.
Keywords
Populism, Cultural Politics, Sweden Democrats, Finns Party, Nordic Model

Introduction
In many Western societies, cultural policy has become increasingly politicised, as the cultural
aspects of politics have become increasingly pronounced (e.g. Harding 2022; Rius-Ulldemolins and
Rubio-Arostegui 2022; Sivonen and Purhonen 2021). This politicisation appears to reflect a broader
shift in political discourse which has been identified in recent research on populism’s impact on
various dimensions of polity, policies and politics (Caiani and Graziano 2022). The
(re)politicisation of cultural policy has been fuelled by the rise of populism, which is increasingly
seen as a significant challenge to established democratic politics (Caramani 2017; Mudde 2019;
Mudde and Kaltwasser 2017; Norris and Inglehart 2019). Nationalist populism, in particular, has
placed strong emphasis on cultural values and identities as the basis for cultural policies (Moran and
Littler 2020).
Populist tendencies have also become visible in the Nordic countries, where cultural policy
structures were broadly established during the emergence of the welfare state after WWII (Mangset
et al. 2008; Sokka et al. 2022). Despite the different historical backgrounds and institutional
contexts of the Nordic countries, they share many similar features that have been categorised as a
distinct ‘Nordic cultural policy model’. This model includes established national and local
administration for cultural services, powerful interest organisations, the application of the arm’s
length principle, and, in some cases, strong legislative frameworks (Kangas and Vestheim 2010;
Mangset 2015; Saukkonen 2021). Consensus-orientation is also a distinct feature: coalition

Abstract
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine profoundly disrupted Arctic governance, challenging the
long-standing notion of Arctic exceptionalism and creating enduring turbulence. While
scholarly debate has largely focused on geopolitical and institutional consequences, the local-
level impacts remain underexamined. This study investigates adaptive governance (AG)
responses to the war’s effects in Norway’s northernmost counties, Troms and Finnmark, which
share a direct border with Russia. The analysis draws on the concepts of crisis, turbulence, and
AG, situating them within broader scholarship on how decision-making сenters respond to
crises and turbulence and political adaptation. It examines stakeholder responses across four
key domains: civilian preparedness, international cooperation, infrastructure development, and
the economic repercussions of sanctions. Based on 19 semi-structured interviews, policy
documents, and media analysis, the study reveals both adaptation and persistent challenges
shaped by pre-existing governance structures, demographic and economic conditions, and past
cooperation with Russia. The study contributes to AG literature by unpacking the interplay
between strategies, highlighting structural constraints, and demonstrating how geopolitical
disruptions shape local governance in strategically significant environments.

peaceful co-existence” (Käpylä & Mikkola, 2015, p. 5). Though widely embraced in scholarship

mobilized, and embedded in dense transnational networks—yet shaped as much

the value of multilevel governance as an integrative framework for contemporary

Abstract
The accelerating impacts of climate change and intensifying geopolitical interests have posi-

ronmental governance. In response, countries with Arctic interests have increasingly adopted
national strategies that articulate security priorities across geopolitical, economic, and environ-
mental dimensions, among others. Yet, despite the growing salience of Arctic security, exist-
ing scholarship remains fragmented and predominantly qualitative, offering limited systematic,
data-driven cross-national comparisons of Arctic strategies. This study addresses these gaps by
examining the Arctic policy documents of the eight Arctic states – Canada, Denmark, Finland,
Iceland, Norway, Russia, Sweden, and the United States – alongside observer states China and
India. Using 107 Arctic policy documents from ten countries and a human-led, AI-assisted
text-mining workflow, we quantify and compare national security priorities across countries.
